claim: Exercise is an effective strategy in the prevention and treatment of metabolic diseases.
source: Exercise is an effective strategy in the prevention and treatment of metabolic diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about exercise benefits.

claim: Alterations in the skeletal muscle proteome, including post-translational modifications, regulate its metabolic adaptations to exercise.
source: Alterations in the skeletal muscle proteome, including post-translational modifications, regulate its metabolic adaptations to exercise.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: HIIT revealed the response of 3168 proteins in human skeletal muscle.
source: Here, we examined the effect of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on the proteome and acetylome of human skeletal muscle, revealing the response of 3168 proteins and 1263 lysine acetyl-sites on 464 acetylated proteins.
evidence: This is directly supported by the proteomic data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIIT revealed the response of 1263 lysine acetyl-sites on 464 acetylated proteins in human skeletal muscle.
source: Here, we examined the effect of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on the proteome and acetylome of human skeletal muscle, revealing the response of 3168 proteins and 1263 lysine acetyl-sites on 464 acetylated proteins.
evidence: This is directly supported by the acetylome data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIIT induced global protein adaptations involved in metabolism, excitation-contraction coupling, and myofibrillar calcium sensitivity.
source: We identified global protein adaptations to exercise training involved in metabolism, excitation-contraction coupling, and myofibrillar calcium sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data and enrichment analyses presented in the results.

claim: HIIT increased the acetylation of mitochondrial proteins, particularly those of complex V.
source: Furthermore, HIIT increased the acetylation of mitochondrial proteins, particularly those of complex V.
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data and enrichment analyses showing mitochondrial and complex V enrichment.

claim: Exercise training is the most effective means to improve cardiovascular fitness and metabolic health.
source: Exercise training is the most effective means to improve cardiovascular fitness and metabolic health, both being predominant determinants of life expectancy and all-cause mortality (Mandsager et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandsager et al., 2018.

claim: Cardiovascular fitness and metabolic health are predominant determinants of life expectancy and all-cause mortality.
source: Exercise training is the most effective means to improve cardiovascular fitness and metabolic health, both being predominant determinants of life expectancy and all-cause mortality (Mandsager et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandsager et al., 2018.

claim: Alterations to the proteome of skeletal muscle underpin its adaptations to exercise training, including glucose and fatty acid metabolism, insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial respiration, immune function, and excitation-contraction coupling.
source: Alterations to the proteome of skeletal muscle underpin its adaptations to exercise training, including glucose and fatty acid metabolism, insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial respiration, immune function, and excitation-contraction coupling (Deshmukh et al., 2021; Egan and Zierath, 2013; Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Holloway et al., 2009; Hostrup and Bangsbo, 2017; Robinson et al., 2017; Ubaida-Mohien et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Proteome-wide post-translational modifications play an important role in regulating metabolism via modulating signaling, protein stability and enzyme activity.
source: Furthermore, proteome-wide post-translational modifications play an important role in regulating metabolism via modulating signaling, protein stability and enzyme activity (Baeza et al., 2016; Cohen, 2000), and are sensitive to exercise stimuli (Hoffman et al., 2015; Overmyer et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baeza et al., 2016 and Cohen, 2000.

claim: Post-translational modifications are sensitive to exercise stimuli.
source: Furthermore, proteome-wide post-translational modifications play an important role in regulating metabolism via modulating signaling, protein stability and enzyme activity (Baeza et al., 2016; Cohen, 2000), and are sensitive to exercise stimuli (Hoffman et al., 2015; Overmyer et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffman et al., 2015; Overmyer et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2020.

claim: In human vastus lateralis muscle biopsies from male athletes, 941 acetylated proteins containing 2811 lysine acetylation sites have been identified.
source: In human vastus lateralis muscle biopsies from male athletes, 941 acetylated proteins containing 2811 lysine acetylation sites have been identified (Lundby et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lundby et al., 2012.

claim: Mitochondria were the cellular component of human skeletal muscle exhibiting the greatest proportion of acetylated proteins.
source: Mitochondria were the cellular component of human skeletal muscle exhibiting the greatest proportion of acetylated proteins (Lundby et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lundby et al., 2012.

claim: Eight untrained men completed a HIIT regimen consisting of 5 weeks of supervised cycling, performed as 4–5×4 min intervals at a target heart rate of >90% max interspersed by 2 min of active recovery, undertaken three times weekly.
source: Eight untrained men (23–38 years of age; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) completed a HIIT regimen (Figure 1A) that consisted of 5 weeks of supervised cycling, performed as 4–5×4 min intervals at a target heart rate of >90% max interspersed by 2 min of active recovery, undertaken three times weekly.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol performed in the study.

claim: Participants experienced a 14% improvement in maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) during HIIT.
source: Participants experienced a 14% and 17% improvement in maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) and incremental peak power output, respectively, during HIIT (Figure 1B and C; p<0.001), which compares favorably to typical HIIT-induced adaptations (Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and C with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Participants experienced a 17% improvement in incremental peak power output during HIIT.
source: Participants experienced a 14% and 17% improvement in maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) and incremental peak power output, respectively, during HIIT (Figure 1B and C; p<0.001), which compares favorably to typical HIIT-induced adaptations (Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B and C with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: The HIIT-induced improvements in V̇O2max and peak power output compare favorably to typical HIIT-induced adaptations.
source: Participants experienced a 14% and 17% improvement in maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) and incremental peak power output, respectively, during HIIT (Figure 1B and C; p<0.001), which compares favorably to typical HIIT-induced adaptations (Wen et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation to Wen et al., 2019.

claim: Participants gained an average of 1.0±0.3 kg lean mass during HIIT training.
source: In addition, participants gained an average of 1.0±0.3 kg lean mass during HIIT training, without changes in fat mass (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: HIIT training did not change fat mass in participants.
source: In addition, participants gained an average of 1.0±0.3 kg lean mass during HIIT training, without changes in fat mass (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The rate of fat oxidation during submaximal cycling (50–150 W) increased following HIIT.
source: The rate of fat oxidation during submaximal cycling (50–150 W) increased following HIIT (Figure 1D), while no apparent changes were observed for carbohydrate oxidation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: No apparent changes were observed for carbohydrate oxidation during submaximal cycling following HIIT.
source: The rate of fat oxidation during submaximal cycling (50–150 W) increased following HIIT (Figure 1D), while no apparent changes were observed for carbohydrate oxidation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: HIIT increased mitochondrial respiration across a range of respiratory states.
source: In line with previous findings (Christensen et al., 2016; Dohlmann et al., 2018; Granata et al., 2016; Jacobs et al., 2013; Larsen et al., 2015; Meinild Lundby et al., 2018), HIIT increased mitochondrial respiration across a range of respiratory states, increasing CI +II coupled respiration by 30% (p<0.001) and electron transport system capacity by 15% (p=0.049) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1F and citations to previous studies.

claim: HIIT increased CI +II coupled respiration by 30%.
source: In line with previous findings (Christensen et al., 2016; Dohlmann et al., 2018; Granata et al., 2016; Jacobs et al., 2013; Larsen et al., 2015; Meinild Lundby et al., 2018), HIIT increased mitochondrial respiration across a range of respiratory states, increasing CI +II coupled respiration by 30% (p<0.001) and electron transport system capacity by 15% (p=0.049) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1F with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: HIIT increased electron transport system capacity by 15%.
source: In line with previous findings (Christensen et al., 2016; Dohlmann et al., 2018; Granata et al., 2016; Jacobs et al., 2013; Larsen et al., 2015; Meinild Lundby et al., 2018), HIIT increased mitochondrial respiration across a range of respiratory states, increasing CI +II coupled respiration by 30% (p<0.001) and electron transport system capacity by 15% (p=0.049) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1F with statistical significance p=0.049.

claim: HIIT induced a robust increase in citrate synthase activity by 42%.
source: Furthermore, HIIT induced a robust increase in citrate synthase activity by 42% (p=0.002) (Figure 1G), a validated marker of mitochondrial volume in human skeletal muscle (Larsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1G with statistical significance p=0.002.

claim: Citrate synthase is a validated marker of mitochondrial volume in human skeletal muscle.
source: Furthermore, HIIT induced a robust increase in citrate synthase activity by 42% (p=0.002) (Figure 1G), a validated marker of mitochondrial volume in human skeletal muscle (Larsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Larsen et al., 2012.

claim: 3343 proteins were identified in skeletal muscle using single-shot DIA.
source: We obtained extensive proteome coverage identifying 3343 proteins (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the proteomic data analysis.

claim: 3168 proteins were quantified within skeletal muscle after filtering.
source: After applying a filter of four valid values out of the eight participants in at least one time point, 3168 proteins were quantified within skeletal muscle (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the proteomic data analysis after applying filtering criteria.

claim: The mean number of proteins quantified per sample was 2853±33.
source: Due to the nature of DIA, few missing values required imputation in each sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; mean proteins quantified per sample: 2853±33).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Good correlation (median correlation: 0.88) between biological replicates was apparent.
source: Good correlation (median correlation: 0.88) between biological replicates (participants at the same time point) was apparent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HIIT regulated 126 proteins (permutation-based FDR <0.05).
source: HIIT regulated 126 proteins (permutation-based FDR <0.05). Of these, 102 proteins were upregulated, while 24 were downregulated (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 102 proteins were upregulated by HIIT.
source: HIIT regulated 126 proteins (permutation-based FDR <0.05). Of these, 102 proteins were upregulated, while 24 were downregulated (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 24 proteins were downregulated by HIIT.
source: HIIT regulated 126 proteins (permutation-based FDR <0.05). Of these, 102 proteins were upregulated, while 24 were downregulated (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIIT upregulated classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins including cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b (COX5B) and NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7 (NDUFA7).
source: These included the upregulation of classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins (e.g. cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b; COX5B & NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7; NDUFA7), as well as proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism (e.g. nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT), branched-chain amino acid metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase; BCKDK) and ubiquinone biosynthesis (5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase; COQ7), the latter of which we have recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle (Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIIT upregulated proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism including nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT).
source: These included the upregulation of classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins (e.g. cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b; COX5B & NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7; NDUFA7), as well as proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism (e.g. nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT), branched-chain amino acid metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase; BCKDK) and ubiquinone biosynthesis (5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase; COQ7), the latter of which we have recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle (Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIIT upregulated proteins involved in branched-chain amino acid metabolism including branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase (BCKDK).
source: These included the upregulation of classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins (e.g. cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b; COX5B & NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7; NDUFA7), as well as proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism (e.g. nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT), branched-chain amino acid metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase; BCKDK) and ubiquinone biosynthesis (5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase; COQ7), the latter of which we have recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle (Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HIIT upregulated proteins involved in ubiquinone biosynthesis including 5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase (COQ7).
source: These included the upregulation of classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins (e.g. cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b; COX5B & NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7; NDUFA7), as well as proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism (e.g. nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT), branched-chain amino acid metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase; BCKDK) and ubiquinone biosynthesis (5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase; COQ7), the latter of which we have recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle (Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021.

claim: COQ7 has been recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle.
source: These included the upregulation of classical endurance exercise training-responsive mitochondrial proteins (e.g. cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5b; COX5B & NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 7; NDUFA7), as well as proteins involved in NAD+ metabolism (e.g. nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT), branched-chain amino acid metabolism (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase; BCKDK) and ubiquinone biosynthesis (5-demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase; COQ7), the latter of which we have recently described in exercise-trained mouse skeletal muscle (Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gonzalez-Franquesa et al., 2021.

claim: Glutaminyl-tRNA synthase (QARS) was amongst the most significantly upregulated proteins within the proteome following HIIT.
source: We also identified novel exercise-training regulated proteins, including, but not limited to, glutaminyl-tRNA synthase (QARS) and rab GDP dissociation inhibitor alpha (GDI1). QARS, which catalyzes the glutamate aminoacylation of tRNA and thus plays a central role in translation (Deutscher, 1984), was amongst the most significantly upregulated proteins within the proteome.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data analysis.

claim: QARS catalyzes the glutamate aminoacylation of tRNA and thus plays a central role in translation.
source: QARS, which catalyzes the glutamate aminoacylation of tRNA and thus plays a central role in translation (Deutscher, 1984), was amongst the most significantly upregulated proteins within the proteome.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Deutscher, 1984.

claim: GDI1 was lowered by HIIT.
source: In addition, GDI1, which inhibits insulin-stimulated glucose uptake by preventing the dissociation of GDP from Rab10 (Chen et al., 2009), was lowered, providing a novel potential mechanism for the insulin-sensitizing effects of exercise training.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data analysis.

claim: GDI1 inhibits insulin-stimulated glucose uptake by preventing the dissociation of GDP from Rab10.
source: In addition, GDI1, which inhibits insulin-stimulated glucose uptake by preventing the dissociation of GDP from Rab10 (Chen et al., 2009), was lowered, providing a novel potential mechanism for the insulin-sensitizing effects of exercise training.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: The lowering of GDI1 provides a novel potential mechanism for the insulin-sensitizing effects of exercise training.
source: In addition, GDI1, which inhibits insulin-stimulated glucose uptake by preventing the dissociation of GDP from Rab10 (Chen et al., 2009), was lowered, providing a novel potential mechanism for the insulin-sensitizing effects of exercise training.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data showing GDI1 reduction and the known function of GDI1.

claim: Enrichment analysis identified the predominant regulation of mitochondrial proteins by HIIT.
source: After filtering for differentially regulated proteins, enrichment analysis using Fisher's exact test indicated the predominant regulation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g. GOCC: mitochondrial part and mitochondrial inner membrane) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hierarchical clustering analysis identified that mitochondrial terms were enriched within the upregulated proteins.
source: Hierarchical clustering analysis on z-scored differentially regulated proteins identified that the mitochondrial terms were enriched within the upregulated proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Summed protein abundances demonstrated mitochondrial biogenesis following HIIT.
source: Summed protein abundances also demonstrated mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 2D), including upregulated protein content of electron transport chain complexes (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), mitochondrially encoded proteins (Figure 2F) and proteins containing a mitochondria-targeting transit peptide (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the summed protein abundance data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HIIT upregulated protein content of electron transport chain complexes.
source: Summed protein abundances also demonstrated mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 2D), including upregulated protein content of electron transport chain complexes (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), mitochondrially encoded proteins (Figure 2F) and proteins containing a mitochondria-targeting transit peptide (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HIIT upregulated mitochondrially encoded proteins.
source: Summed protein abundances also demonstrated mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 2D), including upregulated protein content of electron transport chain complexes (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), mitochondrially encoded proteins (Figure 2F) and proteins containing a mitochondria-targeting transit peptide (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HIIT upregulated proteins containing a mitochondria-targeting transit peptide.
source: Summed protein abundances also demonstrated mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 2D), including upregulated protein content of electron transport chain complexes (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), mitochondrially encoded proteins (Figure 2F) and proteins containing a mitochondria-targeting transit peptide (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The increase in the proteome mirrors the functional increase in mitochondrial respiratory capacity of skeletal muscle after HIIT.
source: Thus, the increase in the proteome mirrors the functional increase in mitochondrial respiratory capacity of skeletal muscle after HIIT (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the proteomic changes to the functional respiratory capacity data.

claim: HIIT did not change skeletal muscle fiber-type composition in terms of myosin heavy chain isoforms.
source: We next investigated whether HIIT influenced the fiber-type proportions of skeletal muscle. While HIIT did not change skeletal muscle fiber-type composition in terms of myosin heavy chain isoforms (Figure 3A) and myosin light chain proteins (Figure 3B), a coordinated regulation of proteins modulating myosin light chain phosphorylation was identified (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HIIT did not change myosin light chain proteins.
source: We next investigated whether HIIT influenced the fiber-type proportions of skeletal muscle. While HIIT did not change skeletal muscle fiber-type composition in terms of myosin heavy chain isoforms (Figure 3A) and myosin light chain proteins (Figure 3B), a coordinated regulation of proteins modulating myosin light chain phosphorylation was identified (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A coordinated regulation of proteins modulating myosin light chain phosphorylation was identified following HIIT.
source: We next investigated whether HIIT influenced the fiber-type proportions of skeletal muscle. While HIIT did not change skeletal muscle fiber-type composition in terms of myosin heavy chain isoforms (Figure 3A) and myosin light chain proteins (Figure 3B), a coordinated regulation of proteins modulating myosin light chain phosphorylation was identified (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased following HIIT.
source: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased concomitantly with a reduction in smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1), an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex (Wooldridge et al., 2008) and an increase in myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A), the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (Alessi et al., 1992; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1) decreased following HIIT.
source: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased concomitantly with a reduction in smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1), an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex (Wooldridge et al., 2008) and an increase in myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A), the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (Alessi et al., 1992; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SMTNL1 is an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex.
source: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased concomitantly with a reduction in smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1), an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex (Wooldridge et al., 2008) and an increase in myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A), the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (Alessi et al., 1992; Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wooldridge et al., 2008.

claim: Myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A) increased following HIIT.
source: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased concomitantly with a reduction in smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1), an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex (Wooldridge et al., 2008) and an increase in myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A), the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (Alessi et al., 1992; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PPP1R12A is the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1.
source: Abundance of myosin light chain kinase 2 (MYLK2) decreased concomitantly with a reduction in smoothelin-like protein 1 (SMTNL1), an inhibitor of the myosin phosphatase complex (Wooldridge et al., 2008) and an increase in myosin phosphatase-targeting subunit 1 (PPP1R12A), the myosin-targeting regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (Alessi et al., 1992; Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alessi et al., 1992.

claim: Reduced MYLK2 abundance was confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: Reduced MYLK2 abundance was confirmed by immunoblotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: These adaptations in proteins regulating myosin phosphorylation have been previously detected in slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers following moderate-intensity continuous cycling training.
source: Furthermore, we have previously detected these adaptations in slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers following moderate-intensity continuous cycling training (Deshmukh et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Deshmukh et al., 2021.

claim: Phosphorylation of myosin light chains promotes myofibrillar calcium sensitivity.
source: Given that phosphorylation of myosin light chains promotes myofibrillar calcium sensitivity (Davis et al., 2001), the reduction in both MYLK2 and SMTNL1 alongside an increase in PPP1R12A indicates an adaptation towards reduced myosin phosphorylation and lowered calcium sensitivity following exercise training.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2001.

claim: The reduction in both MYLK2 and SMTNL1 alongside an increase in PPP1R12A indicates an adaptation towards reduced myosin phosphorylation and lowered calcium sensitivity following exercise training.
source: Given that phosphorylation of myosin light chains promotes myofibrillar calcium sensitivity (Davis et al., 2001), the reduction in both MYLK2 and SMTNL1 alongside an increase in PPP1R12A indicates an adaptation towards reduced myosin phosphorylation and lowered calcium sensitivity following exercise training.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and the known function of these proteins.

claim: Myofibrillar calcium sensitivity decreases following high-intensity sprint training in untrained males, particularly at a low pH representing physiological exercising conditions.
source: Indeed, myofibrillar calcium sensitivity decreases following high-intensity sprint training in untrained males, particularly at a low pH representing physiological exercising conditions (Lynch et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lynch et al., 1994.

claim: Knockdown of Smtnl1 augments exercise training-induced improvements in endurance performance.
source: Although the functional importance of such adaptations remains elusive, knockdown of Smtnl1 augments exercise training-induced improvements in endurance performance, while sedentary Smtnl1-/- mice display a fiber-type switch mimicking endurance exercise training (Wooldridge et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wooldridge et al., 2008.

claim: Sedentary Smtnl1-/- mice display a fiber-type switch mimicking endurance exercise training.
source: Although the functional importance of such adaptations remains elusive, knockdown of Smtnl1 augments exercise training-induced improvements in endurance performance, while sedentary Smtnl1-/- mice display a fiber-type switch mimicking endurance exercise training (Wooldridge et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wooldridge et al., 2008.

claim: HIIT reduced the abundance of L-type calcium channel subunits (dihydropyridine receptor, DHPR).
source: Providing a further link to the altered calcium handling following HIIT (Lynch et al., 1994), we identified a downregulation of L-type calcium channel subunits, otherwise known as the dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: DHPR controls the coupling of membrane depolarization and sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-release in skeletal muscle via its interaction with ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1).
source: DHPR controls the coupling of membrane depolarization and sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-release in skeletal muscle via its interaction with ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) (Flucher and Franzini-Armstrong, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Flucher and Franzini-Armstrong, 1996.

claim: HIIT did not influence the abundance of RYR1.
source: Conversely to DHPR, HIIT did not influence the abundance of RYR1 (Figure 3F) or the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases 1–3 (ATP2A1-3 (SERCAs); Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HIIT did not influence the abundance of sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases 1–3 (SERCAs).
source: Conversely to DHPR, HIIT did not influence the abundance of RYR1 (Figure 3F) or the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases 1–3 (ATP2A1-3 (SERCAs); Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fast-twitch fibers have greater sarcoplasmic reticulum volume, faster calcium release and re-uptake kinetics, and a greater content of DHPR than slow-twitch fibers.
source: Fast-twitch fibers have greater sarcoplasmic reticulum volume, faster calcium release and re-uptake kinetics, and a greater content of DHPR than slow-twitch fibers (Banas et al., 2011; Deshmukh et al., 2021; Murgia et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Banas et al., 2011; Deshmukh et al., 2021; Murgia et al., 2017.

claim: The HIIT-induced reduction of DHPR abundance may represent a slowing of muscle fibers independently of their myosin heavy chain abundance.
source: Thus, the HIIT-induced reduction of DHPR abundance may represent a slowing of muscle fibers independently of their myosin heavy chain abundance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and the known characteristics of fiber types.

claim: A total of 1990 acetyl-sites on 664 proteins were identified in the acetylome analysis.
source: We identified a total of 1990 acetyl-sites on 664 proteins (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the acetylome data analysis.

claim: 1073 acetyl-sites identified in this study were not identified in the analysis of Lundby et al.
source: While this is fewer than the 2,11 acetyl-sites on 941 proteins identified in the largest human skeletal muscle acetylome to date (Lundby et al., 2012), we identified 1073 acetyl-sites that were not identified in the analysis of Lundby et al (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 1263 acetylated sites on 464 proteins were quantified within skeletal muscle after filtering.
source: After applying a filter of 4 valid values out of the seven participants in at least one time point we quantified 1263 acetylated sites on 464 proteins within skeletal muscle (Figures 1G and 4A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is directly supported by the acetylome data analysis after applying filtering criteria.

claim: Six acetyl-sites were quantified exclusively in the pre-HIIT samples.
source: Six and 42 acetyl-sites were quantified exclusively in the pre- and post-HIIT samples, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by the acetylome data analysis.

claim: 42 acetyl-sites were quantified exclusively in the post-HIIT samples.
source: Six and 42 acetyl-sites were quantified exclusively in the pre- and post-HIIT samples, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by the acetylome data analysis.

claim: The mean number of acetyl-sites quantified in each sample was 976.
source: The mean number of acetyl-sites quantified in each sample was 976 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Median correlation between biological replicates in the acetylome was 0.76.
source: Median correlation between biological replicates (between participants at the same time point) was 0.76 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating greater variation in the human acetylome than the proteome, as would be expected (Lundby et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The acetylome displays greater variation than the proteome, as would be expected.
source: Median correlation between biological replicates (between participants at the same time point) was 0.76 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating greater variation in the human acetylome than the proteome, as would be expected (Lundby et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lundby et al., 2012 and the comparison of correlation values.

claim: 421 proteins were quantified in both the proteome and acetylome.
source: There was considerable overlap with proteins quantified in the proteome, with 421 proteins quantified in both (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 1232 of the quantified acetyl-sites were located on the 421 proteins quantified in both the proteome and acetylome.
source: Of the quantified acetylated sites (1263), the majority (1232) were located on these 421 proteins (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Histone H4 (HIST1H4A) had the highest acetylation intensity, making up approximately 10% of the total acetylome intensity.
source: Histone H4 (HIST1H4A) had the highest acetylation intensity, making up approximately 10% of the total acetylome intensity, supporting the regulatory role of histone acetylation in modulating transcription (Sterner and Berger, 2000; Strahl and Allis, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome intensity ranking data.

claim: Histone acetylation plays a regulatory role in modulating transcription.
source: Histone H4 (HIST1H4A) had the highest acetylation intensity, making up approximately 10% of the total acetylome intensity, supporting the regulatory role of histone acetylation in modulating transcription (Sterner and Berger, 2000; Strahl and Allis, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sterner and Berger, 2000; Strahl and Allis, 2000.

claim: One-dimensional enrichment analysis identified mitochondrial terms as enriched for high acetylation intensity.
source: To identify systematic trends in protein acetylation, we performed a one-dimensional enrichment analysis (Cox and Mann, 2012) on the summed protein acetylation intensities, which ranked the proteins by acetylation intensity and identifies Gene Ontology (GO) annotations that are systematically over-represented with higher intensities (positive enrichment factor) and lower intensities (negative enrichment factor). This identified mitochondrial terms (e.g. GOCC: mitochondrial part and mitochondrial matrix) as enriched for high acetylation intensity (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Proteins of carboxylic acid metabolic processes display systematically high acetylation intensity.
source: In particular, proteins of carboxylic acid metabolic processes (e.g. TCA cycle) and monovalent inorganic cation transport (e.g. electron transport chain complex V proteins) display systematically high acetylation intensity (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Proteins of monovalent inorganic cation transport (e.g. electron transport chain complex V proteins) display systematically high acetylation intensity.
source: In particular, proteins of carboxylic acid metabolic processes (e.g. TCA cycle) and monovalent inorganic cation transport (e.g. electron transport chain complex V proteins) display systematically high acetylation intensity (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT) K70 had the highest ACI within skeletal muscle.
source: However, nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT) K70 had the highest ACI within skeletal muscle (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the ACI ranking data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NNT is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein, which uses the proton motive force to maintain high levels of NADPH.
source: NNT is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein, which uses the proton motive force to maintain high levels of NADPH (Hoek and Rydström, 1988) and in doing so can regulate metabolism (Freeman et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoek and Rydström, 1988; Freeman et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2017.

claim: NNT can regulate metabolism.
source: NNT is an inner mitochondrial membrane protein, which uses the proton motive force to maintain high levels of NADPH (Hoek and Rydström, 1988) and in doing so can regulate metabolism (Freeman et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2006; Ho et al., 2017.

claim: NNT is highly acetylated in cardiac muscle.
source: NNT is also highly acetylated in cardiac muscle (Foster et al., 2013), although the effect of acetylation on NNT activity remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Foster et al., 2013.

claim: NNT can regulate acetylation via NADPH-mediated regulation of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) activity.
source: Nonetheless, NNT can regulate acetylation via NADPH-mediated regulation of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) activity (Ho et al., 2017), thus acetylation of NNT may represent a feedback mechanism controlling cellular acetylation and metabolism.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ho et al., 2017.

claim: Acetylation of NNT may represent a feedback mechanism controlling cellular acetylation and metabolism.
source: Nonetheless, NNT can regulate acetylation via NADPH-mediated regulation of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) activity (Ho et al., 2017), thus acetylation of NNT may represent a feedback mechanism controlling cellular acetylation and metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known functions of NNT.

claim: One-dimensional enrichment analysis identified the mitochondria and carboxylic acid catabolic processes to be enriched within higher stoichiometry acetylated proteins.
source: To identify systematic trends in acetyl-site stoichiometry, we performed a one-dimensional enrichment analysis (Cox and Mann, 2012) on acetyl-site ACI using the leading protein ID for relative enrichment (Tyanova et al., 2016). We identified the mitochondria (e.g. GOCC: mitochondrial part and mitochondrial inner membrane) and carboxylic acid catabolic processes to be enriched within higher stoichiometry acetylated proteins (Figure 4G, H and Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins have relatively high stoichiometry acetyl-sites, consistent with analyses in HeLa cells, rodent liver and yeast.
source: This extends previous analyses by not only showing that mitochondrial proteins make up the majority of acetylated proteins in skeletal muscle (Lundby et al., 2012), but also by identifying mitochondrial proteins as having relatively high stoichiometry acetyl-sites – an observation that is consistent with analyses in HeLa cells, rodent liver and yeast (Hansen et al., 2019; Weinert et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2019; Weinert et al., 2014; Weinert et al., 2015.

claim: Proteins involved in contraction were enriched for proteins with low stoichiometry acetyl-sites.
source: Enriched for proteins with low stoichiometry acetyl-sites were proteins involved in contraction (e.g. GOCC: contractile fiber part; Figure 4G, H and Supplementary file 9), including the Uniprot keyword term 'muscle protein' (Figure 4G), which, conversely, was enriched for high-protein acetylation intensity (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Myosin displayed the greatest enrichment for low acetylation stoichiometry.
source: Myosin displayed the greatest enrichment for low acetylation stoichiometry (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Despite contractile proteins displaying high-protein acetylation intensity, they contain acetylation sites of relatively low stoichiometry.
source: Thus, despite contractile proteins displaying high-protein acetylation intensity and making up a substantial number of known acetylated proteins within skeletal muscle (Lundby et al., 2012), they contain acetylation sites of relatively low stoichiometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment analyses comparing intensity and stoichiometry.

claim: The high acetylation intensity of contractile proteins is likely due to high protein abundance and a large number of acetylation sites per protein.
source: The high acetylation intensity of these proteins is therefore likely due to high protein abundance and a large number of acetylation sites per protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing high intensity but low stoichiometry.

claim: Proteins annotated to the cytosol and plasma membrane displayed low acetyl-site ACI.
source: Proteins annotated to the cytosol and plasma membrane also displayed low acetyl-site ACI (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Differences in the inter-organelle acetylation levels of skeletal muscle can likely be explained by subcellular compartmentalization of acetyl-CoA.
source: This highlights differences in the inter-organelle acetylation levels of skeletal muscle and can likely be explained by subcellular compartmentalization of acetyl-CoA (Pietrocola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Pietrocola et al., 2015.

claim: HIIT increased the mean number of acetyl-sites quantified per sample by over 100 sites.
source: HIIT increased the mean number of acetyl-sites quantified per sample by over 100 sites (Pre: 915±44, Post: 1037±51; p=0.015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with statistical significance p=0.015.

claim: 20 acetyl-sites were upregulated and 1 downregulated following HIIT at FDR <0.05.
source: Using a stringent statistical approach of permutation-based FDR corrected paired t-tests, we identified 20 upregulated acetyl-sites and 1 downregulated site (FDR <0.05; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 257 acetyl-sites were upregulated and 26 downregulated following HIIT at Π<0.05.
source: In addition, by applying a validated, albeit less stringent, significance score (Π-value), which combines the statistical significance (p-value) with the fold change (Xiao et al., 2014), we extended this to identify 257 upregulated and 26 downregulated acetyl-sites following HIIT (Π<0.05; Figure 5A and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A using the Π-value approach.

claim: There was a trend for increased acetylation following HIIT.
source: In general, there was a trend for increased acetylation following HIIT (Figure 5A), which could not be explained by changes in protein content as the fold changes in acetylation generally exceeded those of protein abundance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The fold changes in acetylation generally exceeded those of protein abundance following HIIT.
source: In general, there was a trend for increased acetylation following HIIT (Figure 5A), which could not be explained by changes in protein content as the fold changes in acetylation generally exceeded those of protein abundance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in protein acetylation was validated via immunoblotting.
source: The increase in protein acetylation was subsequently validated via immunoblotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hyperacetylation of SOD2 occurred at K68, 75, 122, and 130 in response to HIIT.
source: Within the increased sites, acetyl-sites on metabolic enzymes isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH2), pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 component subunit alpha (PDH1A), succinate CoA ligase subunit alpha (SUCLG1) and ATP synthase coupling factor 6 (ATP5J) were apparent (Figure 5A), while hyperacetylation of SOD2 occurred at K68, 75, 122, and 130 in response to HIIT (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Histone H1.5 (HIST1H1B) K48 showed increased acetylation, despite significantly reduced protein abundance.
source: Interestingly, Histone H1.5 (HIST1H1B) K48 showed increased acetylation, despite significantly reduced protein abundance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fisher's exact test identified the enrichment of mitochondrial and TCA cycle terms within the differentially regulated acetyl-proteins.
source: A Fisher's exact test of HIIT-regulated acetyl-sites (Π<0.05), using leading protein ID for relative enrichment, indicated the predominant regulation of the TCA cycle pathway, mitochondrial proteins (e.g. GOCC: mitochondrial part and mitochondrial inner membrane) and, in particular, electron transport chain complex V proteins (GOCC: mitochondrial proton-transporting ATP synthase complex) (Figure 5C, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A sequence with a predominance of proximal cysteine residues as well as an aspartic acid residue in the +1 position was identified around acetylated lysine residues using iceLogo.
source: To further explore the regulation of HIIT-induced acetylation in skeletal muscle, we looked for consensus sequences around the acetylated lysine residues using iceLogo (Colaert et al., 2009). We identified a sequence with a predominance of proximal cysteine residues as well as an aspartic acid residue in the +1 position (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The aspartic acid at +1 is a feature of mitochondrial acetylated proteins.
source: The aspartic acid at +1 is a feature of mitochondrial acetylated proteins (Lundby et al., 2012) and its enrichment is likely due to the over-representation of mitochondrial proteins in the upregulated acetyl-sites (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lundby et al., 2012 and the enrichment data.

claim: Proximal cysteine residues are associated with promoting non-enzymatic lysine acetylation.
source: Proximal cysteine residues are associated with promoting non-enzymatic lysine acetylation (Hansen et al., 2019; James et al., 2018) via initial cysteine acetylation followed by transfer of the acetyl group to lysine (James et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2019; James et al., 2018.

claim: Non-enzymatic acetylation increases alongside elevated fatty acid oxidation.
source: Indeed, non-enzymatic acetylation increases alongside elevated fatty acid oxidation (Pougovkina et al., 2014), as is apparent in skeletal muscle mitochondria after HIIT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pougovkina et al., 2014 and the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increased non-enzymatic acetylation likely occurs through changes in acetyl-CoA concentration and/or increased acetyl-CoA flux.
source: This likely occurs through changes in acetyl-CoA concentration and/or increased acetyl-CoA flux (Pougovkina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pougovkina et al., 2014.

claim: Acetyl-CoA content within resting skeletal muscle does not change in response to exercise training.
source: Although acetyl-CoA content within resting skeletal muscle does not change in response to exercise training (Putman et al., 1998), acetyl-CoA levels and TCA cycle flux increase during exercise (Constantin-Teodosiu et al., 1991; Gibala et al., 1998; Howlett et al., 1998; Putman et al., 1998), which may result in an accumulation of lysine acetylation during repeated bouts of exercise.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Putman et al., 1998.

claim: Acetyl-CoA levels and TCA cycle flux increase during exercise.
source: Although acetyl-CoA content within resting skeletal muscle does not change in response to exercise training (Putman et al., 1998), acetyl-CoA levels and TCA cycle flux increase during exercise (Constantin-Teodosiu et al., 1991; Gibala et al., 1998; Howlett et al., 1998; Putman et al., 1998), which may result in an accumulation of lysine acetylation during repeated bouts of exercise.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Constantin-Teodosiu et al., 1991; Gibala et al., 1998; Howlett et al., 1998; Putman et al., 1998.

claim: Increased acetyl-CoA levels during exercise may result in an accumulation of lysine acetylation during repeated bouts of exercise.
source: Although acetyl-CoA content within resting skeletal muscle does not change in response to exercise training (Putman et al., 1998), acetyl-CoA levels and TCA cycle flux increase during exercise (Constantin-Teodosiu et al., 1991; Gibala et al., 1998; Howlett et al., 1998; Putman et al., 1998), which may result in an accumulation of lysine acetylation during repeated bouts of exercise.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited evidence about acetyl-CoA changes during exercise.

claim: Acute exercise decreases skeletal muscle acetylation in exercising rats.
source: Conversely, acute exercise decreases skeletal muscle acetylation in exercising rats (Overmyer et al., 2015), but whether this is the case for humans remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Overmyer et al., 2015.

claim: SIRT3 displayed a small but non-significant trend for increased abundance following exercise training.
source: A subset of sirtuins (SIRT2, SIRT3, and SIRT5), a family of protein deacetylases, were quantified in the proteome. SIRT3, a mitochondrial-localized deacetylase, displayed a small but non-significant trend for increased abundance following exercise training (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The abundance of SIRT1 did not change following HIIT.
source: Of the cystosolic and nuclear-localized SIRTs, the abundance of SIRT1 did not change, while SIRT6 increased by 27%.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data.

claim: SIRT6 increased by 27% following HIIT.
source: Of the cystosolic and nuclear-localized SIRTs, the abundance of SIRT1 did not change, while SIRT6 increased by 27%.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data.

claim: SIRT3 increased in abundance by 61% following HIIT.
source: The mitochondrial-localized SIRT3 and SIRT5 increased in abundance by 61% and 32%, respectively, following HIIT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SIRT5 increased in abundance by 32% following HIIT.
source: The mitochondrial-localized SIRT3 and SIRT5 increased in abundance by 61% and 32%, respectively, following HIIT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mitochondrial acetylation increased concomitantly with an increase in the abundance of mitochondrial sirtuins.
source: Thus, mitochondrial acetylation increased concomitantly with an increase in the abundance of mitochondrial sirtuins (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: The protein abundance of the mitochondrial acetyltransferase GCN5L1 was unchanged by exercise training.
source: Conversely, the protein abundance of the mitochondrial acetyltransferase general control of amino acid synthesis 5 like-1 (GCN5L1) was unchanged by exercise training (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SIRT5 displays a preference for desuccinylase and demalyonylase activity rather than deacetylase activity.
source: Although the deacetylase activity of SIRT5 has been questioned, instead displaying a preference for desuccinylase and demalyonylase activity (Du et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2011), SIRT3 appears to play a major role in suppressing non-enzymatic mitochondrial acetylation (Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Du et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2011.

claim: SIRT3 appears to play a major role in suppressing non-enzymatic mitochondrial acetylation.
source: Although the deacetylase activity of SIRT5 has been questioned, instead displaying a preference for desuccinylase and demalyonylase activity (Du et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2011), SIRT3 appears to play a major role in suppressing non-enzymatic mitochondrial acetylation (Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weinert et al., 2015.

claim: Elevated SIRT3 abundance following exercise training might be a mechanism to suppress excess acetylation.
source: Therefore, elevated SIRT3 abundance following exercise training might be interpreted as a mechanism to suppress excess acetylation, either to preserve the activity of mitochondrial enzymes (Hirschey et al., 2010; Tao et al., 2010; Vassilopoulos et al., 2014) or to scavenge acetyl groups for reintegration into acetyl-CoA and energy production.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and cited literature.

claim: Almost every quantified complex V protein had at least one acetyl-site that increased following HIIT.
source: While proteins of complexes I, II, III and IV showed a mixed acetylation response to exercise training, almost every quantified complex V protein had at least one acetyl-site that increased following HIIT (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TCA cycle enzymes displayed high acetylation intensity and stoichiometry in the basal state and HIIT augmented levels of acetylation at every stage of the cycle.
source: Similarly, TCA cycle enzymes, which are localized to the mitochondrial matrix, displayed high acetylation intensity and stoichiometry in the basal state and HIIT augmented levels of acetylation at every stage of the cycle (Figure 6B), again likely due to their proximity to acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cytosolic proteins regulating skeletal muscle contraction showed fewer upregulated acetyl-sites with a number of downregulated sites following HIIT.
source: Conversely, cytosolic proteins regulating skeletal muscle contraction showed fewer upregulated acetyl-sites with a number of downregulated sites following HIIT (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Proteins in close proximity to acetyl-CoA appear to be more susceptible to acetylation.
source: Thus, proteins in close proximity to acetyl-CoA appear to be more susceptible to acetylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the acetylation patterns observed in different cellular compartments.

claim: Median acetylation stoichiometry in rodent liver has been calculated at only 0.05%, which increases slightly to 0.11% for mitochondrial proteins.
source: Median acetylation stoichiometry in rodent liver has been calculated at only 0.05%, which increases slightly to 0.11% for mitochondrial proteins (Weinert et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weinert et al., 2015.

claim: The median log2-fold change for mitochondrial acetyl-sites following HIIT was 0.9.
source: The median log2-fold change for mitochondrial acetyl-sites following HIIT was 0.9 (the corresponding value in the proteome was 0.3), indicating that median post-HIIT stoichiometry would have remained at less than 1%.
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data analysis.

claim: The levels of HIIT-induced changes in acetylation may not be large enough to influence gross activity on most metabolic enzymes.
source: Thus, the levels of HIIT-induced changes in acetylation may not be large enough to influence gross activity on most metabolic enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stoichiometry calculations.

claim: Acetylation of mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (MDH2) negatively correlates with its enzyme activity.
source: Nonetheless, physiological acetylation may be high enough to be regulatory on some proteins. For example, acetylation of mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (MDH2) negatively correlates with its enzyme activity (Overmyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Overmyer et al., 2015.

claim: PDHA1 Lys 336 was within the top 5 most upregulated acetyl-sites with exercise training.
source: Another such enzyme could be pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), whose E1 component subunit alpha (PDHA1) is within the top 25 most acetylated proteins (Supplementary file 6), whilst PDHA1 Lys 336 was within the top 5 most upregulated acetyl-sites with exercise training (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increased acetylation of PDHA1 occurs alongside suppressed enzyme activity in SIRT3 knockout mice.
source: Increased acetylation of PDHA1 occurs alongside suppressed enzyme activity in SIRT3 knockout mice (Jing et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jing et al., 2013.

claim: Exercise-induced hyperacetylation of PDH could play a role in the metabolic switch towards elevated fat oxidation following exercise training.
source: Thus, exercise-induced hyperacetylation of PDH could play a role in the metabolic switch towards elevated fat oxidation following exercise training.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the acetylation data and the known function of PDH.

claim: Mitochondrial hyperacetylation increases fatty-acid-supported respiration.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial hyperacetylation increases fatty-acid-supported respiration (Williams et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2020.

claim: Hyperacetylation of mitochondrial proteins following exercise training may support the bioenergetic adaptations to exercise.
source: These data are consistent with the concomitant increase in acetylation (Figure 5A) and mitochondrial respiratory capacity and fat oxidation (Figure 1F) following HIIT, suggesting that hyperacetylation of mitochondrial proteins following exercise training may support the bioenergetic adaptations to exercise.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlations between acetylation and functional changes.

claim: Increases in certain acetylated histone residues are well characterized to augment transcription.
source: Aside from metabolic enzymes and contractile proteins, histones are regulated by acetylation (Sterner and Berger, 2000; Strahl and Allis, 2000) and may represent a more specifically regulated pool of proteins, owing to the nuclear localization of acetyltransferases (Hendzel et al., 1994). Increases in certain acetylated histone residues are well characterized to augment transcription, with exercise known to acutely regulate H3 acetylation (e.g. H3 K4, H3 K9/14, and H3 K36) (Joseph et al., 2017; Lochmann et al., 2015; McGee et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sterner and Berger, 2000; Strahl and Allis, 2000.

claim: Exercise is known to acutely regulate H3 acetylation (e.g. H3 K4, H3 K9/14, and H3 K36).
source: Increases in certain acetylated histone residues are well characterized to augment transcription, with exercise known to acutely regulate H3 acetylation (e.g. H3 K4, H3 K9/14, and H3 K36) (Joseph et al., 2017; Lochmann et al., 2015; McGee et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Joseph et al., 2017; Lochmann et al., 2015; McGee et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2008.

claim: 18 distinct acetylated peptides from histones were identified.
source: Here, we identified 18 distinct acetylated peptides from histones, with acetylated peptides from H1.5 (HIST1H1B K48), H2B type 2 F (HIST2H2BF K16/20), and H3.3 (H3F3B K23) being elevated following HIIT (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Acetylated peptides from H1.5 (HIST1H1B K48), H2B type 2 F (HIST2H2BF K16/20), and H3.3 (H3F3B K23) were elevated following HIIT.
source: Here, we identified 18 distinct acetylated peptides from histones, with acetylated peptides from H1.5 (HIST1H1B K48), H2B type 2 F (HIST2H2BF K16/20), and H3.3 (H3F3B K23) being elevated following HIIT (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the acetylome data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Acetylation of the N-terminal of H2B, including K16 and K20, has been linked to transcriptional activation.
source: However, acetylation of the N-terminal of H2B, including K16 and K20, has been linked to transcriptional activation (Chen et al., 2014; Parra et al., 2006), including the expression of NAD-metabolic genes in yeast (Parra et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2014; Parra et al., 2006.

claim: Acetylation of H3 K23 contributes to the development of cancer through the recruitment of the transcription factor TRIM24 and the nuclear receptor estrogen receptor alpha (ERS1).
source: The role of H3 K23 is also obscure, however, its acetylation contributes to the development of cancer through the recruitment of the transcription factor transcription intermediary factor 1-alpha (TRIM24) and the nuclear receptor estrogen receptor alpha (ERS1) (Lv et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2010), augmenting expression of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-biphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha (PIK3CA), a subunit of phosphoionositide-3-kinase (PI3K), and phosphorylation of protein kinase B (AKT1) (Lv et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lv et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2010.

claim: TRIM24 promotes the abundance of glycolytic and TCA cycle genes in transforming human mammary epithelial cells.
source: Indeed, TRIM24 promotes the abundance of glycolytic and TCA cycle genes in transforming human mammary epithelial cells (Pathiraja et al., 2015), while ERS1 regulates mitochondrial biogenesis in skeletal muscle (Ribas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pathiraja et al., 2015.

claim: ERS1 regulates mitochondrial biogenesis in skeletal muscle.
source: Indeed, TRIM24 promotes the abundance of glycolytic and TCA cycle genes in transforming human mammary epithelial cells (Pathiraja et al., 2015), while ERS1 regulates mitochondrial biogenesis in skeletal muscle (Ribas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ribas et al., 2016.

claim: HIIT increased the protein abundance of EP300 by 23%.
source: Similarly to the upregulation of acetylation on H2B K16/20 and H3 K23, HIIT increased the protein abundance of EP300 by 23% (participant 1 was excluded as an outlier; Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Knockdown of EP300 reduced acetylation of H2B K20 by 48%.
source: Knockdown of EP300 reduced acetylation of H2B K20 by 48%, whilst acetylation of H3 K23 was unaffected (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Knockdown of EP300 did not affect acetylation of H3 K23.
source: Knockdown of EP300 reduced acetylation of H2B K20 by 48%, whilst acetylation of H3 K23 was unaffected (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: EP300 is an exercise-training responsive acetyltransferase, which regulates the acetylation of H2B K20 in skeletal muscle.
source: Together, these analyses identify EP300 as an exercise-training responsive acetyltransferase, which regulates the acetylation of H2B K20 in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EP300 upregulation data and the knockdown experiment results.
